http://www.russiaherald.com/news/2792632.text: Ukraine has morphed into Zelensky's 'concentration camp' - Moscow RT.com 25 Aug 2026, 07:14 GMT+10 Kiev has descended into repression at home and "outright terror" against Russian civilians, Moscow's UN envoy has said Ukraine has been transformed into a "Zelensky concentration camp" with Western assistance, Russia's envoy to the UN, Vassily Nebenzia, has said, accusing Kiev of suppressing dissent at home and increasingly resorting to attacks on civilians in Russia. Nebenzia made the remarks at a UN Security Council meeting on Monday marking the 35th anniversary of Ukraine's declaration of independence. The session was requested by the Council's five European members - Denmark, France, Greece, Latvia and the UK - who reiterated their full political and military support for Kiev. The Russian diplomat questioned whether Ukraine had anything to celebrate, arguing that successive governments had run the country "into the ground" and that Vladimir Zelensky had accelerated the process. "With the most active involvement of the countries of the collective West, which claim to be 'civilized' and 'democratic,' Ukraine has morphed into a 'Zelensky concentration camp,' where any dissent or opposition is completely prohibited and those who find the courage to voice an alternative point of view are thrown behind bars without trial or due process, or physically eliminated," he said. Nebenzia described the persecution of the canonical Ukrainian Orthodox Church, the glorification of Nazi collaborators, and the suppression of shared history and the Russian language - including a comical ban on a popular Russian cartoon - as a "vivid illustration of the sheer wretchedness of Kiev's rulers." Amid a growing crackdown on dissent and a deteriorating battlefield situation , Kiev has now slipped into "outright terror against Russia's civilian population," Nebenzia argued. "Terror has become the last resort for Kiev in its attempt to reverse the situation that is not currently in its favor," the diplomat said. "At the same time, Zelensky continues to beg his Western patrons for new shipments of weapons and ammunition, which are then used to hit Russian cities, residential areas and civilian infrastructure." READ MORE: Three minors dead after Ukrainian attack on childcare center - official The envoy said at least 475 Russian civilians were killed or injured in Ukrainian attacks between August 10 and 16 alone, with 69 fatalities, including children. He highlighted a strike on Nizhnekamsk that killed 13 people and wounded 78, as well as attacks in Novorossiysk, the Rostov Region and multiple towns in Donbass, which Kiev claims as its territory. "It appears that Ukraine's Western patrons, not to mention Zelensky himself, still harbor the dangerous illusion that further escalation, strikes deep inside our territory and terror against civilians will somehow force us to accept an ultimatum that is being pushed under the guise of peace," he said. The Russian envoy insisted that Moscow retains the battlefield initiative and rejected calls for a temporary ceasefire that he said would merely give Kiev time to regroup and its Western sponsors time to rearm it. He warned that there would be no meaningful diplomatic process as long as Russia is confronted with ultimatums and threats while the realities on the ground are ignored. Photograph: Atef Safadi/EPA West Bank Israeli forces overwhelmed by violent settlers in ‘terrorist attack’ on Palestinian family Settler violence in West Bank makes everyday life ‘untenable’ for Palestinians, says ICRC after assault on family trying to return home in Jalud Emma Graham-Harrison in Jerusalem Wed 30 Sep 2026 10.54 EDT First published on Wed 30 Sep 2026 10.05 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) has said Israeli settler violence in the West Bank has made everyday life for Palestinians “untenable”, as a mob attack on Palestinians trying to return home prompted one of Benjamin Netanyahu’s main rivals to warn of a campaign of settler terror. More than 100 militant settlers overwhelmed Israeli security forces early on Tuesday to attack a Palestinian family as they attempted to reclaim their homes which had been seized by settlers in the West Bank village of Jalud. Three Israeli security officials were injured and houses were set on fire. The impotence of the Israeli military, the scale of the assault and the injuries inflicted on Israeli security officers by settlers prompted unusually harsh condemnation from Israeli politicians and commenters. Israel is facing unprecedented international pressure over surging violence in the occupied West Bank, where settler militants backed by cabinet ministers have accelerated a campaign of ethnic cleansing ahead of Israel’s elections next month. Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, condemned the attacks in Jalud as a “moral stain”. Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief and Netanyahu’s leading challenger in the upcoming elections, called for action to halt a “campaign of terror and violence”. Deadlier attacks by Israeli settlers, including ones targeting Palestinian children, have drawn less attention inside Israel. “Palestinian rights or safety are not the concern, even for people who are in the opposition,” said Mairav Zonszein, a senior analyst on Israel-Palestine with International Crisis Group. “The settler violence is an issue [for them] because it’s making Israel look bad, and also the idea that the military is losing control.” View image in fullscreen A Palestinian family were attacked as they attempted to reclaim their homes which had been seized by settlers in Jalud. Photograph: Atef Safadi/EPA The ICRC said attacks, settlement expansion and severe restrictions on movement were making everyday life untenable for Palestinian civilians, who Israel has a responsibility to protect under international law. . “The frequent and severe violence must be brought to an end,” said Julien Lerisson, the head of the ICRC’s delegation for Israel and Palestine. “What international humanitarian law says on the protection of private and public property, and on the population’s access to essential services, must be respected.” A graphic showing number of Palestinians killed in the West Bank by settlers or Israeli civilians A bar on imports of settlement goods came into force in the Netherlands last week, the UK has announced plans for even broader controls on trade and financing of settlements, and a similar bill will be introduced in the US legislature on Thursday. ‘The settlers brought the violence’: the ethnic cleansing of a West Bank village Read more On Tuesday, a Senate bill demanding a human rights report on Israel’s occupation of the West Bank was narrowly defeated after winning backing from all but one Democrat. “Tonight a disaster was averted, but the barrier has been broken,” the Israeli analyst Roy Sharon wrote on social media after the vote, warning that “anarchy in the West Bank” may cost Israel military aid from the US and its international legitimacy. A cartoon in Israel’s largest-circulation newspaper, Yedioth Ahronoth, on Wednesday showed two soldiers watching an arson attack on a Palestinian home. “They’re going to ruin my trip to Amsterdam,” one says to the other. More than 60 Palestinian communities in the occupied West Bank have been wiped off the map since October 2023 and 18 others have been partly displaced, according to the Israeli rights group B’Tselem. Nearly 5,000 people have been forced from their homes, almost half of them children. View image in fullscreen Mahmod Tubasi, 60, and his wife, Aedah, 51, and their family had been forced out of their homes this summer by settler militants. Photograph: Ammar Awad/Reuters The Tubasi family, whose homes were burned in Jalud, had been forced out this summer after a weeks-long siege by settler militants. Last week they secured a high court ruling ordering the Israeli state to evict settlers and secure their return. Late on Monday the Israeli military told the family that about 15 military police officers would escort them home immediately, Israel’s Haaretz newspaper reported. That was a small number given that Israel is celebrating the Sukkot holiday. The number of violent extremists in illegal settlements usually rises during festivals, and the force was outnumbered by a violent crowd within minutes of arriving. “To carry out an operation such as this, and during the holiday of Sukkot when the [settler] outposts are packed, is madness,” a security source said. The military had not informed national police and the Shin Bet domestic intelligence service of their plans, so they had no security backup. Settlers attacked a house when the Tubasi family arrived, forcing them to the roof, before the military decided to evacuate them in armoured military vehicles. The crowd then set the homes on fire, blocked roads and threw stones at Israeli security forces, injuring three personnel. The two houses “were damaged beyond description”, said Wael ​Tubasi. “They damaged everything – the doors, the tiles were removed, the stairs were removed. They smashed the bathrooms, doors and windows. They left nothing, everything was broken,” he told Reuters. View image in fullscreen The Tubasi family’s homes were ‘damaged beyond description’, said Wael Tubasi. ‘Everything was broken.’ Photograph: Ammar Awad/Reuters Earlier this year the former prime minister Ehud Olmert called for the international criminal court to intervene to stop settler violence because the state had failed. Netanyahu condemned the “violent riots” and called for prosecution of the attackers, but defended the illegal settler movement. “The handful of rioters are not representative of the law-abiding settler public in Judea and Samaria,” the prime minister said, using an Israeli term for the occupied West Bank. A landmark 2024 ruling from the UN’s international court of justice found that the occupation violated international law, a position the British government has endorsed. An Israeli military spokesperson said two suspects had been detained, and called for action to tackle settler militants who targeted Israeli security forces. “The violence directed at soldiers while they were carrying out their duties crosses a clear red line and is unacceptable,” the spokesperson said. “There is no place for such incidents in the state of Israel, and they must not be allowed to become the norm. Such phenomena must be addressed at their root.” On Wednesday, some in Israel questioned whether the army and the state had the capacity to do that. “We have to look reality squarely in the eye: this was a terrorist attack and a failure by the Israeli defence establishment in its entirety,” Avi Ashkenazi wrote in the Maariv newspaper. “It is clear at this point that the real sovereign in Judea and Samaria are the extreme rightwing terrorist activists.” Explore more on these topics West Bank Palestine Israel International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) Middle East and north Africa news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story UN adds 61 firms to settlements blacklist over alleged human rights violations against Palestinians Senior UK rabbis come out in support of sanctions on Israeli settlements Miliband rejects chief rabbi’s claim that West Bank sanctions put UK Jews at risk Will UK sanctions have any impact on Israel’s ‘settler terrorists’ in West Bank? Photograph: Dmitri Lovetsky/AP View image in fullscreen A painting depicting Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping is unveiled in St Petersburg, Russia. Photograph: Dmitri Lovetsky/AP Russia Yalta became a byword for betrayal. Will Trump, Xi and Putin enact another carve-up? Russia and US approach potential summit seeking China’s help to extricate them from wars of choice, as Putin hopes to find consensus on new global order Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor Sat 14 Nov 2026 02.00 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google T he Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, is among those who have expressed concern that the world will witness a Yalta 2.0 moment if Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin meet trilaterally, as expected, on the sidelines of the Apec summit in China next week. It is a truism in diplomacy that if you are not around the table, the risk is that you, or your values, are on the menu and about to be carved up. Many excluded from the summit in Shenzhen, principally Ukraine but also eastern Europe and Baltic countries, Taiwan and even Iran, have reason to be nervous that their sponsors might abandon them in a complex geopolitical trade-off that Putin envisions, and Trump seems to endorse. Putin has long proposed this re-enactment of the greatest wartime summit, held in February 1945 at Joseph Stalin’s insistence in a rundown Tsarist resort on the south coast of Crimea alongside Franklin D Roosevelt and Winston Churchill. Trump has cast himself in the role of the enthusiastic guest while Xi acts the bashful host, ever reluctant to embrace the status of a traditional global superpower. No one quite knows what will happen if the three men meet or even if China will allow more than a stiff protocol-driven exchange of statements. China is already trying to push nuclear disarmament off the agenda. It may prove to be little more than abbreviated geopolitical theatre that Putin can retail domestically to show that Russia – even with an economy seven times smaller than that of the EU – still plays with the big boys. View image in fullscreen The three world leaders are expected to hold a meeting on the sidelines of the Apec summit in Shenzen. Photograph: Yin Haixiang/VCG/Getty Images But if Putin has his way he will try to ensure that this becomes the first of a series of meetings in this format in which the big powers organise a new world order on a set of security oriented principles in which liberal values play little part. As Russia’s chief negotiator, Vladimir Medinsky, told Russian TV: “The task is to create a comprehensive system of comprehensive security in Europe that will become a new modern Yalta or Potsdam. If we manage to create such a security system then we will ensure peace in Europe for decades, perhaps even centuries. That is our main task.” Russia’s foreign ministry spokesperson, Maria Zakharova, said the summit could mark “the start of a return from this slide into absolute chaos to stabilisation”. For Zelenskyy, the concern is that almost any time Putin and Trump converse, it is Kyiv that suffers. The original Yalta is widely remembered, outside Russia, as a moment of cynical trade-offs, even ignominy, to rival the appeasement of the 1938 Munich agreement. It was eight days that shaped the postwar world in which absent countries were discarded or divided by the imminent wartime victors. FDR, months from death, was intent on enlisting Russian support for a new League of Nations organisation and for Russian participation in the war against Japan. In return, he accepted the fait accompli of Russia’s presence in Poland, and covered his treacherous tracks by persuading Stalin to sign a declaration that affirmed the principles of “sovereign rights and self-government” should prevail in countries freed from Nazi rule. Few thought the dictator had any intent to honour the agreement. Indeed, honour was somewhat absent throughout the eight days. When Churchill told Stalin it was a “matter of honour” that the independence of Poland, Britain’s original casus belli , was preserved, Stalin replied the issue for him was “a matter of life and death”. Churchill had no means to confront Stalin since by then he was the victor of Stalingrad and Kursk, and the commander of an army that had crushed Germany. View image in fullscreen Winston Churchill, Franklin D Roosevelt and Joseph Stalin at the Yalta summit in 1945, where the postwar world was shaped. Photograph: Fine Art Images/Heritage Images/Getty Images The subsequent sense of shame about the betrayal of Yalta accumulated mostly in America, so much so that in May 2005, before a trip to Moscow for the 60th anniversary of Victory in Europe Day, George Bush told an audience in Latvia that Yalta had “consigned millions to communist captivity. When powerful nations negotiated, the freedom of small nations was somehow expendable. Yet this attempt to sacrifice freedom for the sake of stability left a continent divided and unstable.” It was a view shared across Europe. The Republican tradition expressed by Bush has been expunged by Trump. In his 2025 national security document, Trump lauded the sphere of influence geopolitics championed at Yalta. He named the western hemisphere as America’s domain. It remained deferential to Russia and China’s spheres. Unfortunately, Trump took little notice of the strategy prepared for him. He retained his respect for Putin and Xi, but indulged himself, and Israel, in a disastrous imperial overreach elsewhere, notably in Iran . skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Thing Our US morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion As a result, the US and Russia are approaching the summit seeking China’s help to extricate them from wars of choice that have wounded them. Xi is cast in the role of Stalin, hosting two countries in need of his beneficence. It leaves China somewhat wary, reluctant to use its leverage if it helps the US, or is seen to run counter to the Chinese narrative of being a force for stability and coexistence. Speaking at the Emirates Policy Center conference in Abu Dhabi, Prof Minghao Zhao from Fudan University gave a classic exposition of Chinese non-interference. “The Russia-Ukraine war is the strategic mistake made by the Russian president. The Iran war is the strategic mistake made by President Trump. China is managing the consequences of those conflicts.” View image in fullscreen Trump, Putin and Xi as matryoshkas, the traditional Russian wooden dolls. Photograph: Dmitri Lovetsky/AP By contrast, Dr Wang Huiyao, the president of the Center for China and Globalization and an early advocate of a trilateral summit, argued China was needed. He referenced the Kindleberger trap – a period of chaos caused by too little global leadership. He said China was trying to be helpful by propping up multilateralism and might provide guarantees in Iran, something the Iranian leadership favours, but even he saw China’s stabilisation role largely through the prism of developing the global economy. In short, China might help extricate Trump in the Middle East. After all, open waterways are necessary to meet its insatiable demand for oil. But China sees Ukraine as a strictly European security issue in which it is not willing to betray Putin, or endorse a settlement reached without Europe’s agreement. China is in the midst of repairing relations with Europe after China’s industrial overcapacity in 2025 flooded the European market, risking its deindustrialisation. China’s embrace of Putin’s vision of a new European security architecture would infuriate Germany and the European Commission. For some, such as John Ikenberry, the theorist of liberal internationalism, the sight of the US president carving up the world with autocrats is anathema. He thinks there is a viable alliance of democracies. But Charles Kupchan, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, says more Yaltas are the future. “We have to learn to work across the geopolitical and ideological dividing lines,” he said. “We are now in a world in which the US and its democratic allies are no longer the preponderant coalition. “Who is coming up? China, India, Indonesia, large countries of the global south – all of then playing the field and most of them have closer economic ties with China than with the US. “We are going to have to learn to work with autocracies and to live with them more comfortably. Is there a downside risk? Sure. Might Trump throw Taiwan and Ukraine under the bus? Possibly, but I doubt it. But we need to break the ice. These conversations have to start now and I give credit to President Trump for starting it.” Explore more on these topics Russia China Donald Trump Xi Jinping Vladimir Putin Ukraine Iran features Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

(Reuters/Marie Mannes) SPONSORED ARTICLES How logistics industry experts plan to ‘move forward’ after COVID-19 Reasons why Filipinos love Korean culture and products Why Batangas is the destination for budget-friendly family holidays Delhaize stores hit by “IT incident” in Belgium and Luxembourg Sweden’s national cybersecurity centre says it is investigating local incidents Belgian SPAR stores, and Estonian supermarkets also affected STOCKHOLM/BRUSSELS — Ahold Delhaize AD.AS and Colruyt COLR.BR said on Monday that an IT incident overnight hit fridges and freezers in dozens of stores in Belgium and Luxembourg, while Swedish grocers ICA and Coop reported similar temperature spikes, with one store blaming a cyberattack. The incidents follow an attack in France last month, in which police said hackers seized control of cooling units at hundreds of supermarkets, raising temperatures as high as 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit) and causing fires and food losses. Ahold also reported a cybersecurity incident to Dutch police last month after it detected suspicious activity in its infrastructure. On Monday, the Delhaize supermarket chain realized there were temperature increases in the cooling systems, Delhaize spokesperson Sarah De Meester said. The company is investigating the incident. Stephan Moelans, the CEO of Belgian refrigeration company Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize’s systems, told the Belga news agency that the incident was a cyberattack, in which the units’ evaporators were switched to defrost mode. Moelans’ office declined to comment when contacted by Reuters. A spokesperson for Colruyt Group, which operates Spar stores in Belgium under a franchise system, said five shops had their fridge systems attacked. From refrigerators and heating systems to security cameras and alarm networks, an expanding range of devices once largely mechanical can now be monitored and controlled remotely, creating new opportunities for cybercriminals. Authorities have not indicated who could have been behind last month’s incidents. There were no claims of responsibility. Swedish stores also affected The head of Sweden’s national cybersecurity centre, John Billow, told Reuters it was working on several incidents regarding refrigeration systems in grocery stores around Sweden. One Swedish ICA store said on social media that the temperature of its refrigerators and freezers had been “hacked” overnight and set to 50 degrees Celsius. It said later that the store had since opened. At an ICA Baronen store in Stockholm, a notice said all the shop’s freezers were broken due to a cyberattack. The store’s sales manager said the attack happened at 2 a.m. (0100 GMT) and was noticed at 5.30 a.m.. “We are aware that a limited number of stores were affected by an incident overnight, which impacted their refrigeration and freezer systems,” a spokesperson at privately held ICA said in an email. Privately held grocery retail group Coop told Swedish daily Aftonbladet that six of its stores had been affected by similar incidents. It did not immediately respond to a request for comment. “We have in recent weeks… identified that we have quite a lot of exposed operational technology devices in Sweden that we have been clear about the necessity to update or patch,” the cybersecurity centre’s Billow said. An Estonian supermarket chain was also affected, with temperatures set to 50 degrees, technology supplier Kitman Coldtech told public broadcaster ERR. “This is very fresh, it happened this morning,” Kitman CEO Jann Mutso told ERR. He declined to name the affected grocery chain. —Reporting by Anna Ringstrom, Louise Rasmussen and Johan Ahlander in Stockholm; Inti Landauro in Brussels; editing by Terje Solsvik, Kirsten Donovan Interaksyon Investigators hunt French supermarket fridge hackers, no claim of responsibility Baguio tourists reminded of city ordinances amid NCR long weekend China commits to early conclusion of South China Sea code, Philippines says Timor-Leste PM catches attention for cheerful interaction with ASEAN Summit performers Hollywood salutes Glenn Close and Ridley Scott with honorary Oscars Eurovision Asia: A diverse and spectacular showcase of Asian pop Boracay’s Puka Beach welcomes new resort with underwater suites Chinese premier lauds ‘extraordinary’ ties with ASEAN ahead of Trump visit

https://hvg.hu/itthon/20261116_csepel-li.text: A rendőrök a sofőrt elfogták, társát, a lopás elkövetőjét jelenleg is keresik. A helyszínről a mentők két embert súlyos sérülésekkel szállítottak kórházba. Elgázolták a csepeli Lidl parkolójában az üzletlánc egyik dolgozóját vasárnap délután, amikor egy férfi után futott, aki nem sokkal korábban lopott a boltból, majd megpróbált elmenekülni. A Budapesti Rendőr-főkapitányság (BRFK) a 24.hu megkeresésére azt közölte, hogy a lopást követően az elkövető kijött az üzletből, majd egy másik férfi mellé beszállt egy autóba. Ekkor az áruház egyik alkalmazottja kifutott az üzletből, hogy megállítsa az elkövetőt, a mozgó jármű azonban elsodorta. A dolgozót a mentők kórházba vitték. A jármű pár perc múlva egy másik autóval összeütközött, sofőr és a lopás elkövetője ezután elhajtottak. A sofőr azonban rövidesen visszatért a helyszínre, így őt a rendőrök elfogták, illetve sérülései miatt a mentők kórházba szállították, társát jelenleg is keresik. A szemle során a rendőrök az autóban kábítószer-fogyasztásához használt eszközt találtak, ezért a sofőrtől mintát vettek, melyet szakértők bevonásával vizsgálnak. Az esettel összefüggésben a BRFK lopás miatt szabálysértési eljárást, illetve segítségnyújtás elmulasztása és járművezetés bódult állapotban bűncselekmények gyanúja miatt büntetőeljárást indított, vizsgálják az eset körülményeit. Az Országos Mentőszolgálat a lapot arról tájékoztatta, hogy a helyszínről egy 40 év körüli férfit és egy 30 év körüli férfit súlyos sérülésekkel szállítottak kórházba. Akár 15 év börtönt is kaphat a korrupciós pénzt több ügyféltől is a gyanú szerint elfogadó hivatali dolgozó.

Photograph: Kai Pfaffenbach/Reuters Deutsche Bank Deutsche Bank dismissed warnings about dealings with risky clients, reports claim International investigation using trove of leaked internal data allegedly shows German bank overlooked compliance concerns to safeguard profits Kalyeena Makortoff Banking correspondent Tue 17 Nov 2026 08.35 EST First published on Tue 17 Nov 2026 08.34 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Deutsche Bank reportedly dismissed warnings about its dealings with risky clients, including high-profile Russian oligarchs, to protect profits, the findings of an investigation into a trove of leaked bank documents indicate. A leak of 15m internal files is reported to show that the troubled German bank repeatedly ignored concerns by its compliance officers about its risk-taking, despite having already been caught being used to launder billions of dollars for Russian criminals, spies and oligarchs between 2010 and 2015. The investigations, which were published by media outlets including Der Spiegel, the Financial Times, the New York Times and Le Monde, will represent a fresh blow for Deutsche Bank, which has struggled to repair its reputation after a number of scandals and dealings with controversial clients including the US president, Donald Trump, and the sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Deutsche Bank said on Tuesday that the issues raised in the investigations “date back many years, in some cases as much as two decades” and had been addressed by its leadership. “Where relevant, we reviewed these matters at the time and worked closely with regulators.” However, the reports suggested Deutsche Bank prioritised profit ahead of internal controls, and continued to expand its Russian business until 2021, despite warnings from internal compliance officers and growing geopolitical tensions between Nato allies and Moscow. Deutsche Bank allegedly resisted pulling out of Russia even after the Kremlin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, before the bank did a U-turn and exiting the country in March that year. The investigations suggested Deutsche Bank was driven by competitive pressure, including from American banks, and that its chief executive, Christian Sewing, pursued a growth strategy that involved doing business with a list of customers known as its “most sensitive clients”. That covered roughly 50 corporate clients ranked by how close they were to the Kremlin, and other potential risks including financial crime, according to the Financial Times. Some names allegedly on that list included: Russia’s state-owned gas company Gazprom; petrochemicals group Sibur; and oligarchs including the aluminium magnate Oleg Deripaska, the report said. Outside its Russian dealings, the German lender is facing fresh scrutiny for allegedly processing almost $600m (£454m) of suspicious payments linked to Epstein, much higher than previously known. Deutsche said it “regrets [its] historical relationship” with Epstein and that it had made “considerable investments in strengthening controls”. The lender is also accused of accidentally leaking Trump’s tax documents to another client during his first term in office, which Deutsche Bank allegedly kept secret from the White House. Deutsche Bank said it did not comment on former or existing client relationships. Deutsche Bank cut ties with Trump in 2021. The reports prompted a 4% drop in Deutsche Bank’s German-listed shares on Tuesday. Deutsche Bank issued a public statement in response to the investigation on Tuesday, saying it had “gone through a fundamental transformation” under Sewing. “We made substantial investments in our control environment while restoring sustainable profitability, as evidenced by record profits in 2025 as well as in recent quarters. This involved €7bn of direct investments in our control environment between 2019 and 2025.” The bank added: “We remain committed to ensuring continuous enhancements of our control environment and a culture of integrity and completing any outstanding remediation.” “Regardless of how the information was obtained, it includes confidential information about clients, employees and other third parties, which remains legally protected. We have acted, and will continue to act, decisively to protect this,” the bank said.
